why.say:
• Three owners: the client owns the case, Atty. Thorne owns the judgment, the Case Manager owns the movement
• The job shapes whether a case settles well, not just phones and paper
• Example split: deciding to settle is the attorney's; getting the MRI report into the file is the Case Manager's
• One line never to cross: no legal advice, covered in the rules slide
• Red flag: a note to Atty. Thorne with the subject line "Update"; the ask gets buried, and the SOL doesn't wait

theory.say:
• Case Management: keeping the case moving from first call to final check, phase by phase
• Three tests for every task: on time, documented in the file, everyone who needs to know is told
• Case health analysis: reading the whole file for risk, not one task at a time
• Spot weak points early, like a missed deadline, a silent client or a gap in treatment

frame.say:
• Six stages: intake and case opening, planning, documentation, communication, monitoring, billing and resolution
• Intake includes the Conflict Check: making sure the firm doesn't already represent the other side
• Planning: Case Manager drafts the Case Plan; Atty. Thorne sets strategy
• Communication: update client, insurers and doctors, log every contact the same day; monitoring: every deadline calendared
• Documentation is where cases most often stall; missing records delay the demand

rules.say:
• Case Manager owns deadlines, documents, insurers, doctors and client updates
• Atty. Thorne owns every legal judgment: value, strength, strategy, whether to settle
• Log every contact, document and deadline in the CMS the same day; if it isn't in the CMS, it didn't happen
• Allowed: explain the process, confirm facts; never: tell a client the case value or whether to take an offer
rules.ask: A client asks whether to take the offer. What do you say?

model.say:
• Case lifecycle, eight stations: Intake, Claim Set-Up, Treatment, Pre-Demand, Demand, Settlement and Liens, Disbursement, Litigation
• Liens: bills paid out of the settlement before the client gets their share
• Litigation is dashed: the path only taken if the case doesn't settle
• Navy band: Case Manager owns the movement; orange band: Atty. Thorne owns every legal judgment
• The CMS sits under station one because the whole track runs on it

job.say:
• New case assigned: read the raw file in the CMS first, noting every party, date and insurer before calling
• Client asks a legal question: log it in the Communications Log, create a task, route to Atty. Thorne same day
• Deadlines and risks go on the Calendar and under Risk Flags, each with a next step
• Adjusters read the file history; a clean, logged file signals the firm is organized and ready
job.ask: What is the first thing you check on a brand-new file?

why.say:
• Every new file raises the same questions: who was hurt, when, who is insured, for how much, what could go wrong
• All week, every lesson and Learning Check works one file: John Doe v. Robert Smith
• Know its facts cold so every CMS step makes sense
• One detail on this file changes how much money John Doe can reach
• Red flag: any snapshot field with no document behind it isn't verified, even John's seat; name the document or mark it not yet verified

theory.say:
• Case Snapshot: the file's ID card with parties, date of loss, statute of limitations, client position and insurance
• Statute of limitations: the legal deadline to sue
• Facts of Loss: how, where and when, backed by the Police Report and witnesses
• Critical Case Event: the one fact the defense builds on; spot it early for Atty. Thorne
• Sources: intake sheet, supplement, Police Report; quote the document, never memory

frame.say:

why.say:
• Intake is where the Case Manager takes control of the file, not just data entry

map.say:
• Opening a file runs in six steps, in order, on day one

• 4 Map every role and client seating; 5 insurance from the Dec Page; 6 name and file every document

theory.say:
• Recovery Stack: every policy that can pay the claim, in the order it pays; find every layer at intake
• Bodily Injury Liability (BI): the at-fault driver's coverage for injuries to others; pays first, a third-party claim
• UM/UIM: coverage when the at-fault driver has no or not enough insurance; first-party, from the client's car or household
• Exclusions and signed UM rejections can close a layer; record the exact document that did it

theory2.say:
• MedPay and PIP: medical coverage from the client's side that pays regardless of fault, early in the claim
• Property Damage liability and collision cover cars only; neither joins the injury stack
• Split limit, e.g. 25/50: first number caps each injured person, second caps the whole accident; read both
• Declaration Page (Dec Page): the insurer's own statement of insureds, cars, coverage and limits; the only proof

frame.say:

why.say:
• The Case Plan is the file's instruction manual; Atty. Thorne sets strategy from it
• A plan that hides a risk builds the strategy on a false picture
• Example: John Doe's 14-day Treatment Gap belongs in the plan; opinions about him or case value do not
• Red flag: a Risks band that says "none" for a client nobody has examined isn't clean, it's buried
• No treatment yet means the days keep counting; every open risk gets its source and its date

theory.say:
• Early evaluation answers three questions: is there money, who is responsible, how will the case move
• Coverage determination: which policies apply, their benefits, limits and exclusions
• Liability assessment: who caused the crash; clear, shared or disputed; on what evidence
• Case projection: early read on risk and direction; case value always stays with the attorney
• Strict compliance: every plan deadline goes on the calendar

frame.say:
• Coverage: is there money? Valid policies, coverage type, limits, exclusions, gaps
• Liability: who is responsible and how much? Includes comparative negligence: the client sharing some blame
• Projection: how will the case move? Draws on coverage, liability, injury, expected treatment, paperwork quality
• Projection comes last because it depends on the other two

rules.say:
• Decide acceptance: Accepted, Escalated or Declined, with a reason others can follow; no file left in limbo
• Projection stays preliminary until coverage is confirmed; liability needs the Police Report, statements, any video
• Hold a place for the Regulatory Triple-Check, cleared in the Treatment Phase
• File the plan within the state's window, often 30 to 60 days, and calendar it
• Every goal gets a measure, owner, date; flag bad facts loudly; value is Atty. Thorne's

model.say:

why.say:
• There is no such thing as full coverage; every policy pays a different thing
• Keep two questions separate: who pays the bills now, and who pays the claim later
• Payer-First Principle: each bill goes to the payer that must pay it first
• Wrong order: the bill returns as a lien, paid from John Doe's settlement
• Red flag: a stack that adds up to $45,000 means PIP slipped in; PIP pays bills, not the claim
• The stack is BI $10,000, Host UM $20,000 and Relative UM $10,000: $40,000, every time

theory.say:
• Every policy: whose is it, and what does it pay?
• Third-party coverage belongs to the at-fault driver, Robert Smith; first-party answers to the client's side
• Recovery Stack: only coverage that pays the claim: BI (bodily injury on the at-fault driver), then UM/UIM
• MedPay and PIP: no-fault medical coverage paying accident bills fast, regardless of fault
• UM follows the person, not the car; John Doe has no car policy

theory2.say:
• Set-off and non-duplication: some policies subtract what PIP or MedPay paid; verify in writing
• Subrogation: a payer's right to be repaid from the settlement
• Contract rate and write-off: in-network providers accept the Health Plan's price, so the lien is smaller
• Medicare Secondary Payer: Medicare pays last, is repaid by law, case reported to the BCRC
• Bill first the payer with no right to be repaid

frame.say:
• BI liability: at-fault driver's, third-party, pays the injury claim
• UM/UIM: client's side, through vehicle or household, pays when BI is too small; consent rules apply
• PIP: from the vehicle the client rode in, pays Medical Bills without proving fault; verify repayment terms in writing
• Health insurance: client's plan, contract rate, right to be repaid
• Medicare and Medicaid: last, repaid by law, BCRC report

rules.say:

• Sort by what it pays: only BI and UM make the $40,000 stack; Harbor Point PIP $5,000 pays bills

• Bill order: PIP (no repayment right, confirmed 03/02/2026), Health Plan, then Letter of Protection

theory.say:
• Claim set-up is coverage determination: which policies apply, how much they pay, what they exclude

theory2.say:

frame.say:

why.say:

frame.say:

• Measurable: a standard scale, e.g. range of motion, pain or disability score, sessions attended
• Achievable: set by the doctor's outlook, never the claim; Relevant: tied to injuries, daily life, work
• Time-bound: a check-in date, e.g. the 12-week review
• The doctor sets the medical target; we write the goal into the Case Plan

rules.say:
• Assess the whole person, starting from the intake call and Run Report
• Medical findings in his words and the record's, never your diagnosis
• Ask about living situation, transport, cost, and every prior injury, claim and doctor; request those records
• Record what his job demands physically
• Build doctor-confirmed SMART goals, map the four care groups, calendar every risk; coordinate care, never prescribe

• Record the four-area assessment in Case Notes, each area dated, unknowns as open questions
• Prior injury: request records through Medical Records Requests; write body part, dates, doctor, outcome
• In the Action Plan Editor, write SMART goals and care groups under Clinical and Functional pillars
• Each with a measure, date and owner; ask the first doctor to confirm
• Calendar life barriers, like no ride, as treatment risks

dodont.say:
• Do: record the assessment in his own words, dated, beside the Run Report's "neck stiffness"
• Do: ask about prior injuries early; write "none ordered" with a date for empty care groups
• Don't: build the plan from records only, ignoring transport or his Northgate job
• Don't: set goals like "reduce pain" with no measure or date
• Don't: call a prior condition unrelated or aggravated; that is the doctor and Atty. Thorne's call
dodont.ask: What question would you ask John Doe to learn how he was before the crash?

why.say:
• Adjusters, IME doctors and defense lawyers compare John Doe's records to a standard map of recovery
• IME: an exam by a doctor the insurer hires
• Care drifting off the map is the top reason insurers deny treatment and order an IME
• Red flag: no visit from 04/02 to 04/21/2026, nineteen days, with no reason on file
• Run A-C-T the same day, and his reason goes to Atty. Thorne

theory.say:
• Standard Treatment Map: ambulance and ER, imaging, chiropractic and therapy, orthopedics and pain management, surgery only if serious
• A skipped or out-of-order stop needs a medical reason on file
• Clinical Pathway: is he improving? If not, variance loop, figuring out why; next steps are the doctor's decision
• Reasonable and Necessary: the insurer's payment test; normal care for the injury, and is he actually doing more

theory2.say:
• 6-Week Rule: by week 6, expect 20 to 30 percent more range of motion or lower pain; otherwise raise it
• Red Flag Rule: no disability score change after 12 weeks is a plateau; specialist or second opinion is the doctor's call
• Objective metrics: Oswestry or DASH every 30 days, walking test, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 when stalled, FCE before return to work
• Stakeholder Triad: clinic, lawyer and insurer, with the Case Manager passing information

frame.say:
• Acute, days 1 to 14: ER or urgent care, imaging, brace; focus on causation and lining up PIP
• Sub-acute, weeks 2 to 8: active therapy two or three times a week, specialists; watch range-of-motion gains
• Restorative, weeks 9 to 24: work hardening, injections, emotional support; look for return-to-work blockers
• Maintenance, six months on: home exercises; question is MMI, Maximum Medical Improvement
• Discharge, maybe an impairment rating; every treatment is a doctor's order, never ours

rules.say:
• Count phase from the date of loss and weeks of care from the first visit; place him on the map every check-in
• If not improving, name the problem type: clinical, psychosocial (life or mood), or systemic (stuck approvals, booked clinics)
• Systemic delays are never the client's fault
• Get doctor's measurements on file; raise concerns at week 6 and the 12-week plateau; real red flags go into A-C-T
• Doctor decides care; Atty. Thorne decides what it means for the case

model.say:
• At intake John Doe had one medical record: the EMS Run Report from 02/06/2026
• It notes neck stiffness and that he declined transport, so no ER stop
• He was in the acute phase with no care; every day without evaluation is a fact on the timeline
• Tell Atty. Thorne about any gap; focus on causation facts and Harbor Point's $5,000 PIP confirmed in writing
• Later: attendance, week-6 measurements, return-to-work blockers, the doctor's MMI note

job.say:
• At each check-in, record in the CMS treatment timeline: phase, week from date of loss, week of care, improving or not, date
• If not improving or a stop is skipped, label the problem type, call the doctor's office, note the plan in Case Notes
• Request measurements at week 6 of care and every 30 days after
• Claim-threatening problems: same-day Risk Flag to Atty. Thorne, facts only

dodont.say:
• Do: write phase and week at the top of every note
• Do: report what he can't do, not just diagnoses; request objective measures before week 6
• Don't: let care drift without a reason on file, or call a systemic delay client non-compliance
• Don't: wait for a denial to course-correct; call the provider that same week
• The map is a measuring stick; off the map is fine once the doctor explains it
dodont.ask: Counting from 02/06/2026, what date does the acute window close, and what must be on file?

why.say:
• A client who never calls is a risk; silence is where cases fall apart
• At intake John Doe had no treatment; only the 02/06/2026 EMS report: neck stiffness, declined transport
• Once care begins, the Case Manager reads every record and hears from him between visits
• Missed flags or stalls can pull him off his doctors' plan and leave Atty. Thorne without facts
• Red flag: "Missing visits will hurt your case" is advice; talk logistics and his reasons, and what it means goes to Atty. Thorne

map.say:
• Read records for red flags, warning signs, by specialty: physical therapy, surgery, medication, mental health
• Listen on calls for yellow flags: life and mood problems blocking recovery, written in his words
• Talk using OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries
• At the plateau, when progress and interest drop, bring him back to his own goal
• Route it: medical danger to the doctor, legal to Atty. Thorne; then A-C-T: Assess, Coordinate, Track

theory.say:
• Know standard treatment patterns to spot when care goes off track
• Red flag: a departure from the pattern signaling medical danger, a stuck case, or over-treatment for billing
• Physical therapy flags show stalling or over-treatment; surgery flags concern safety and standard of care
• Pain management and medication get the most scrutiny, due to opioid rules and necessity audits
• Medical danger goes to the doctor same day; legal danger to Atty. Thorne

theory2.say:
• Mental health and head-injury claims must be tied to the crash and confirmed by a doctor
• Yellow flags: fear-avoidance (afraid to move), catastrophizing (expecting the worst), lawsuit stress, relying on pills or passive care
• Yellow flags are mostly heard on calls, not read in records
• Motivational interviewing: drawing out the client's own reasons to keep going
• Mid-treatment plateau: early motivation fades and attendance drops unless someone re-engages him

frame.say:
• Physical therapy: over 12 sessions with no gain and no referral; or only heat, TENS, massage with no exercise
• Surgery: recommended before therapy or injections outside an emergency
• After surgery: fever, redness or sharp pain is medical danger; the doctor hears today
• Medication: opioid, muscle relaxant and sedative together, rising doses, or drug test mismatches
• Mental health: vague life-stress notes, or head-injury symptoms first reported months later

rules.say:
• Read every note against the watch-list; report flags, the doctor judges them
• Therapy: no gain after 12 sessions, passive-only care, two or more missed visits
• Surgery: simpler care skipped, left/right mix-ups, post-surgery symptoms left to the follow-up
• Medication: raise the opioid-relaxant-sedative combo, rising doses, test mismatches with the prescriber as facts, not accusations
• Date every mental health symptom; record yellow flags in his words; at the plateau, revisit his goal

model.say:
• Open question: "Walk me through how your neck has been since the collision"
• Affirmation: recognize effort, e.g. "Nice work getting that first appointment booked"
• Reflection: repeat back what was heard; Summary: pull the call together, ask what was missed
• If therapy feels pointless, set it beside his goal of full shifts at Northgate and let him answer
• If he resists a clinic, don't argue; ask why and take the reason to the doctor

job.say:
• Read every treatment record, prescription record and bill against the red-flag list
• Log any flag in Risk Flags with its source record and date first seen
• Medical danger: call the doctor's office same day, note it in Case Notes, run A-C-T, tell Atty. Thorne
• Check-ins run on OARS; yellow flags in his words; GIRP note (goal, intervention, response, plan) same day
• Dated logs show when the firm knew

dodont.say:
• Do: ask specific questions about visits, pain score, and what he can do at work
• Do: write yellow flags in his own words with the date; raise medication facts with the provider, never as accusations
• Don't: argue with resistance or warn that missed visits hurt his case
• Don't: report a yellow flag with no plan or follow-up date, or treat late head-injury symptoms as proof
• The Case Manager listens and engages; never decides tests, medications or referrals
dodont.ask: Which yellow flag might show up for John Doe, and what open question would uncover it?

why.say:
• PIP: the client's own insurance paying Medical Bills regardless of fault, written state by state
• Florida's Emergency Medical Condition (EMC) rule decides early whether PIP pays $2,500, $10,000, or no medical
• John Doe's file is in Riverton: add-on PIP, no EMC rule, so Harbor Point's $5,000 PIP isn't capped
• On a Florida file, the clock starts at the date of loss; the Case Manager calendars it
• Red flag: telling a Riverton client his PIP is capped over the 14 days; Riverton has no EMC rule

rules.say:
• Florida PIP, Fla. Stat. 627.736: $10,000, paying 80% of reasonable medical and 60% of lost income
• Initial care within 14 days of the accident, or PIP pays no medical
• Full $10,000 only if an MD, DO, dentist, PA or APRN finds an EMC; otherwise capped at $2,500
• EMC: injury serious enough that going without care could seriously harm health; chiropractors can't find one
• Example: a 02/06/2026 Florida loss makes 02/20/2026 day 14; always confirm the current statute
rules.ask: A Florida client is first seen on day 14 by a PA. What does PIP pay?

job.say:
• At intake, calendar the 14-day initial-care deadline from the date of loss
• Tell the client the deadline and where care is available: facts and logistics, no medical recommendation
• First record: check the date against day 14, the provider, and a written EMC determination; request it if missing
• Track the $2,500 or $10,000 bucket in the PIP Log, the record of every PIP payment
• Missing EMC or late first visit goes to Atty. Thorne same day
job.ask: A Florida client first sees a chiropractor on day 10. What's covered, and what's missing?
